stances.claim: Biden's inauguration amid a divided United States is itself an oxymoron, and his vow to unite is historic -- to restore order, revive the rule of law, heal pandemic wounds, win over the 74M who did not vote for him, lift the country from depression, reverse Trump's immigration policies, and regain abandoned-ally trust.
stances.confidence: asserted with 'is he up to the job?' suspended question

stances.claim: Biden's biography of poverty, stutter, family tragedy, undistinguished law standing (76th of 85), repeated failed presidential bids, and Beau's death -- culminating in a 2020 victory at age 78 as oldest US president and second Catholic ever -- qualifies him for the Lincoln-style task ahead.

Biden's life mirrors Lincoln's structurally: child labor at 7, orphaned at 9 by mother, rejected marriage proposal at 28, elected to Congress only on third try at 37, defeated for Senate at 45, failed VP run at 47, finally president at 51 -- and Lincoln 'with malice towards none' forgave Confederate leaders without punishment, then was assassinated by a Confederate sympathizer.

Like Lincoln, Biden in his inaugural address offered reconciliation and unity to the 74M who did not vote for him -- 'We must end this uncivil war that pits red against blue, rural versus urban, conservative versus liberal. We can do this -- if we open our soul instead of hardening our hearts.'

Amanda Gorman's inaugural poem at age 22 -- 'while democracy can be periodically delayed, it can never be permanently defeated. We will not march back to what was. But move to what shall be, a country that is bruised, but whole. Benevolent, but bold. Fierce and free' -- should be celebrated by all peace-loving peoples of the world.

notable_anecdotes: Biden's law-school standing as the most disarming biographical detail -- 'finishing law unexceptionally, ranking 76th in a class of 85' -- used to humanize the eventual president rather than burnish him.

The Dec 18, 1972 detail -- Neilia and one-year-old Naomi killed in an automobile accident 'while shopping for a Christmas tree' -- turning a date into a domestic detail and underlining what Biden survived.

The structural-parallel mapping with Lincoln rendered as a numbered age-by-age timeline (7, 9, 28, 37, 45, 47, 51), one of the most explicit biographical-correspondence devices in this set of columns.

Lincoln's narrow 40%-of-four-candidates popular-vote victory and the Southern rejection both popular and electoral -- a chosen reminder that legitimacy crises preceded the actual Civil War, useful for the Trump-context analogy.

Amanda Gorman quoted at length -- 'a country that is bruised, but whole. Benevolent, but bold. Fierce and free' -- alongside CJ's own one-word benediction 'Amen!' -- a rare moment where CJ explicitly aligns his closing register with a contemporary American voice rather than legal authority.

one_paragraph_summary: On Joe Biden's inauguration as the 46th American president amid a divided United States -- the column's titular oxymoron -- Panganiban catalogs Biden's vows to restore order, revive the rule of law, heal pandemic wounds, win over the 74 million who did not vote for him, lift the country from depression, reverse Trump's immigration policies, and regain abandoned-ally trust. He sketches Biden's life in dot-leader fragments: born to poor Irish-descent parents; mocked as a child for stuttering; window-washing and gardening to pay for high school; ranking 76th of 85 in law school; widowed in 1972 when Neilia and one-year-old Naomi were killed shopping for a Christmas tree; suicidal grief; remarriage to Jill in 1977; six Senate terms; 1987 plagiarism withdrawal; 1988 brain-aneurysm surgery; 2007 caucus exit at under 1%; eight years as Obama's VP; 2015 exit on Beau's death; 2020 victory at age 78, oldest US president ever and only the second Catholic. He then maps Biden's tragedies and triumphs onto Lincoln's structurally -- child labor at 7, orphaned at 9, rejected marriage at 28, Congress on third try at 37, Senate defeat at 45, VP failure at 47, presidency at 51 -- recalling Lincoln's narrow 40% victory among four candidates, the Confederate rejection both popular and electoral, his 'with malice towards none' forgiveness of Robert E. Lee and the Confederate leadership, and his assassination by John Wilkes Booth, a Confederate sympathizer 'who could not accept they lost the war.' Like Lincoln, Biden offered reconciliation in his inaugural -- 'We must end this uncivil war that pits red against blue, rural versus urban, conservative versus liberal. We can do this -- if we open our soul instead of hardening our hearts.' CJ closes with Amanda Gorman's inaugural poem at 22 -- 'a country that is bruised, but whole. Benevolent, but bold. Fierce and free' -- and an 'Amen!': 'may the USA be an oxymoron no more.'
